sections.overview: The southern common cuscus is a nocturnal, tree-dwelling marsupial of southern New Guinea and Cape York Peninsula in northern Australia, where it is also called the grey cuscus. It was long treated as a form of other common cuscuses and is now recognised as a species of its own.
sections.identification: A small to medium-sized cuscus with a head and body of 33–40 cm, a tail of 28–35 cm and a weight of 1.5–2.2 kg. The back is grey-brown with a stripe from head to rump, and the underside is off-white. In New Guinea females are redder brown than the greyer males. Its skull and molars are smaller than those of the northern and eastern common cuscuses.
sections.habitat: In New Guinea it lives in secondary forest, riverside gallery forest, gardens and some degraded areas of the southern lowlands. In Australia it is known from rainforest and vine forest in the Iron Range and McIlwraith Range area on eastern Cape York Peninsula.
sections.diet: In Australia it has been recorded eating the fruit of red cedar, flowers of corky bark and leaves of various trees, and one stomach held seed paste from the black bean tree. Its diet in New Guinea is not described in the source consulted.
sections.behavior: It is nocturnal, sheltering by day in tree hollows, and is believed to be solitary. In Australia it is scarce: spotlighting typically turns up about one animal every two to five hours. Home range and movements are not documented in the source consulted.
sections.reproduction: Very little is known. In Australia, both single young and twins have been recorded. Breeding season, gestation and pouch life are not given in the sources consulted.
sections.ecology: Pythons are thought to be significant predators of the species. Its role in the forest as an eater of fruit, seeds and leaves, for example in dispersing seeds, has not been studied in the sources read.
sections.conservation: It is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List, according to the Mammal Diversity Database and a species treatment, which cite its wide range, presumed large population, presence in protected areas such as Iron Range National Park and tolerance of some habitat change. It is also listed in CITES Appendix II.
